vignette:
He is 51, a South Eastern Asian man who has spent most of his adult life believing that endurance is a private virtue. He works as a tax inspector, a job that suits the part of him that likes order, documentation, and rules that can be followed if one is careful enough. He is married now, but when he speaks about the beginning of the trauma, he goes back to a previous long-term romantic relationship that lasted several years and unraveled behind closed doors in ways he still struggles to name out loud.

At first, he tells himself it is only temper. His partner is charming in public, quick-witted, affectionate after arguments, and skilled at making him feel that he is somehow the cause of every conflict. The first time she hits him, they are in the kitchen late at night after a dispute about money. She throws a mug that shatters near his shoulder, then slaps him hard across the face when he turns away. He remembers standing still, more stunned than hurt, hearing the refrigerator hum and thinking, with absurd clarity, that the neighbors must not hear. The next day he goes to work with a swollen cheek and says he walked into a cabinet door. He repeats the story so evenly that even he nearly believes it.

The violence becomes part of the architecture of daily life. She pushes him into walls, claws at his arms, strikes him with whatever is near at hand. Several times she blocks the doorway so he cannot leave during arguments. Once she corners him in the bedroom and kicks him after he falls against the bedframe, and he curls in on himself, not because he thinks fighting back is wrong in some abstract sense, but because he is terrified of what it would mean if anyone ever saw a man like him admit that he is afraid of his partner. He begins monitoring the apartment the way he later describes reviewing a suspicious tax file: looking for patterns, warning signs, discrepancies in tone. He learns the sound of her footsteps, the significance of a drawer closing too hard, the danger in a too-careful silence.

He becomes smaller in his own life. At work he is still meticulous, arriving early, reviewing records, writing clean notes in the margins of files, but he finds himself startled by raised voices in the office. If a colleague drops a stack of folders, his body jolts before his mind catches up. He keeps extra shirts at work because she has scratched him through the collar before, and he becomes practiced at explaining bruises as clumsiness. He stops inviting friends over. He calls his family less often. Shame settles in him heavily, not only because of the abuse but because he cannot fit his experience into the story he has been taught men are allowed to tell. He thinks he should be able to manage it, contain it, correct it.

The relationship ends only after an assault that frightens him into seeing that he may not get to quietly endure forever. During an argument, she strikes him repeatedly with a metal object from the living room side table and then tells him, while he is bleeding from above the eyebrow, that if he tells anyone, no one will believe him. What lodges in him is not just the pain but the certainty in her voice. He goes to urgent care and again lies about the cause. Not long after, he leaves.

Years pass. He eventually marries a woman he describes as kind and steady. He builds a life that from the outside looks calm. Yet the old fear remains active beneath the surface, as if his body never received the message that the danger ended. He sleeps lightly and wakes at small noises, instantly alert. If his wife reaches for him unexpectedly while he is concentrating, he flinches before he can stop himself, then feels ashamed and overexplains. During marital disagreements, even ordinary ones, his chest tightens and his thoughts scatter. He becomes intensely focused on escape routes, on the position of doors, on keeping his voice level. If she speaks sharply, even briefly, he feels himself pulled backward into the old apartment, his body bracing for impact while part of his mind knows this is not the same person, not the same room.

He avoids television scenes of domestic conflict. He changes the subject when coworkers joke about “crazy exes.” He has never told most people what happened. The secrecy isolates him, but speaking feels dangerous in a way he cannot reason himself out of. Sometimes, while reviewing case documents at work, he catches himself staring at a line of numbers without comprehension because he has drifted into a vivid fragment of memory: the shattered mug, the blocked doorway, the metallic smell of blood. On those days he becomes more rigid, more exacting, as if precision can hold him together.

With his wife, he wants closeness, but fear often arrives first. He checks locks at night more than once. He scans parking lots before walking to his car. He carries himself with the quiet restraint of someone still trying not to provoke a blow that is no longer coming. What troubles him most is that he understands, intellectually, that his present life is safe, yet his body continues to live by the rules of an earlier captivity.
